finding.claim: Broken authorization: update_doc calls can_edit() but discards its boolean result, so the edit check is never enforced. Any caller can overwrite any document's body. The sibling handler update_title correctly uses require_edit().
finding.source: Any request to PUT /doc/<doc_id> with a JSON body {"body": ...}; the doc_id is attacker-chosen and the caller needs no ownership or editor rights.
finding.sink: doc["body"] = request.json["body"] at docs.py:20, a write to the shared DOCS store.

trace.note: Route PUT /doc/<doc_id> is registered with no auth decorator.
doc = DOCS[doc_id] loads the document for the attacker-supplied id.
can_edit(g.user, doc) returns False for a non-editor, but the return value is ignored and abort(403) is never reached.
doc["body"] is overwritten with attacker-controlled content.

finding.guards_checked: require_edit (docs.py:11) would abort with 403, but this handler does not call it. No before_request or auth decorator exists in the file. g.user is never set here, so it presumably comes from external middleware, and that middleware would only authenticate the caller; it would not check per-document authorization. No other check sits on the path.

verdict.guard_found: can_edit() at docs.py:7 returns a bool and is called as a bare statement at docs.py:19, so its result is discarded. require_edit() at docs.py:11 aborts with 403 but is not called in update_doc. The file has no before_request hook or auth decorator.
verdict.reason: docs.py:19 calls can_edit(g.user, doc) as a bare statement and ignores the returned bool, so the write at docs.py:20 runs for any caller, unlike update_title, which calls require_edit at docs.py:27.
